titre: The Night Sky Should Have Been Blinding
accroche: In an infinite universe filled with stars, every line of sight should end on a bright surface. Night should be a wall of light.
contenu_vulgarise:
On a cloudless night, far from any city, the sky stays black between the stars. This blackness long seemed to go without saying. It does not: if the universe is infinite, static, and uniformly populated with stars, then any direction of sight should sooner or later run into the surface of a star. The entire sky should shine like a wall.

## An Old Problem, Misnamed

The reasoning goes back at least to Johannes Kepler, who raises it as early as 1610, then to Edmond Halley and to the Swiss astronomer Jean-Philippe Loys de Chéseaux in the eighteenth century. The name history settled on, “Olbers' paradox,” comes from a physician and amateur astronomer from Bremen, Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers, who in turn formulates it on May 7, 1823, being neither the first nor the most rigorous.

Olbers proposes an explanation: interstellar dust would absorb the light of distant stars, darkening the sky. The British astronomer John Herschel, son of William Herschel, shows that the idea does not hold: dust that absorbs that much light would end up heating and radiating itself, until it shone in its turn. The problem remains intact at Olbers's death in 1840.

## What the Darkness Measures

The right track comes from elsewhere. In 1848, the writer Edgar Allan Poe suggests, in a lecture and then in the essay *Eureka*, that the universe may not be infinite in time: light takes time to travel, so we can only see the stars close enough for their light to have had time to reach us. The intuition is right, but it goes largely unnoticed.

It is the cosmologist Edward Harrison who, in 1964, formalizes the solution accepted today: what matters is not so much the size of the observable universe as the limited lifetime of stars. A sky filled to infinity with eternal stars would indeed be blinding, but stars are born, shine for a measurable time, then go out, which leaves immense volumes of darkness between the active sources of light. Harrison discovers after the fact that Poe, and then Lord Kelvin in 1901, had already glimpsed the essentials.

The blackness of the night sky is therefore not an anomaly to be explained. It is a measurement: it says that the universe has an age, that stars have a lifetime, and that light, however fast it travels, has not had time to bring us everything. What is missing from the sky says as much as what is in it.

repere.texte: Heinrich Olbers formulates the paradox on May 7, 1823, in Bremen. It will take one hundred forty-one years, until Edward Harrison's work in 1964, for an explanation to hold: the finite lifetime of stars, not the absorption by dust that Olbers had first proposed.
repere.source: Biteau, Domínguez, Valls-Gabaud et al., The Conversation, 2023

carte.punch: An infinite universe of eternal stars would make night as bright as day.
carte.idee: If the universe were infinite and static, populated with endless stars, every line of sight would run into a star, and the entire sky should shine. What saves the night is the limited lifetime of stars, established by Edward Harrison in 1964.

quiz.question: Why is the night sky not entirely bright, when an infinite universe of stars would lead us to expect it?
choix: Because interstellar dust absorbs the light of distant stars
Because most stars are too small to be seen with the naked eye
Because Earth's atmosphere blocks the light of the most distant stars
Because stars have a limited lifetime, which leaves vast volumes of darkness between them
quiz.explication: Olbers's explanation, dust absorbing the light, was refuted as early as the nineteenth century: dust that absorbs that much light would end up radiating in turn. The atmosphere and the apparent size of stars do not change the reasoning, which concerns an infinite universe of point sources. It is the finite lifetime of stars, demonstrated by Edward Harrison in 1964, that explains the darkness between them.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who first put forward reasoning close to the paradox, well before Olbers posed it in 1823?
choix: The German astronomer Johannes Kepler, as early as 1610
The cosmologist Edward Harrison, as early as 1848
The writer Edgar Allan Poe, as early as 1823
The British astronomer John Herschel, as early as 1610
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The reasoning goes back at least to Johannes Kepler in 1610, then to Edmond Halley and Jean-Philippe Loys de Chéseaux, before Olbers in turn formulated it in 1823.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why was Olbers's explanation, interstellar dust absorbing light, rejected?
choix: Because no interstellar dust has ever been detected in space
Because dust that absorbs that much light would end up radiating itself
Because Olbers himself retracted this explanation before his death in 1840
Because starlight does not pass through interstellar dust
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The astronomer John Herschel showed that dust absorbing that much light would heat up and end up radiating in turn, which invalidates Olbers's explanation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What intuition does Edgar Allan Poe put forward in 1848 in the essay Eureka?
choix: That the brightest stars mask the light of fainter stars
That the human eye perceives only a fraction of the light actually emitted at night
That the universe may not be infinite in time, since light takes time to travel
That the night sky is dark solely because of Earth's rotation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Poe suggests in Eureka that the universe may not be infinite in time: light takes time to travel, so we see only the stars close enough for their light to have reached us.
